draft.title: Care for Country
card: For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, Country means the land, waters, sky, living things and stories of a place, and the people's bond with them. People belong to Country and have a duty to look after it.
This care has been practised for tens of thousands of years. It is passed on through law, story, song and ceremony, and it draws on close knowledge of seasons, plants and animals.
Cultural burning is one practice. Knowledge holders light small, cool fires at chosen times of year to clear undergrowth, renew plants and protect important places.

Today this knowledge informs land and fire management in Australia. Many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander rangers and land councils work with governments on parks, fire planning and the care of waterways.
draft.remember: Care for Country is a duty to look after land, water and life, built on knowledge passed down over a very long time and now used in land and fire management.

a.q: Which statement best describes what Country means to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples?
opts: Land, waters, living things and stories, with a duty of care
The area of land that a person or family legally owns
Wild areas of bush that have not yet been used by people
The border of a national park managed by a government
a.why: Country includes land, waters, sky, living things and stories, and people have a duty to care for it. It is not just ownership of a block of land, which is the most tempting wrong option, because Country is about relationship and responsibility.
a.clue: Think of a bond and a duty, not just a place on a map.

b.q: A fire agency in New South Wales asks a group of Aboriginal rangers to help plan fire management in a forest. Why is this a sensible step?
opts: Their knowledge of fire, seasons and plants is long held
Their fires would remove all risk of bushfire in the forest
Their work would replace the need for other fire planning
Their methods only work in forests that have never burned
b.why: Care for Country practices draw on knowledge of seasons, plants and fire passed down over a very long time, so it can inform fire planning. It does not remove all risk or replace other planning, as the card says it informs land and fire management, and the most tempting wrong option overstates this.
b.clue: The card says this knowledge informs management, not that it replaces it.

a.best: Land, waters, living things and stories, with a duty of care

b.best: Their knowledge of fire, seasons and plants is long held

problems.detail: All three wrong options use absolute or overstated wording ('remove all risk', 'only work', 'replace the need'), while the right option is the only measured one. A test-wise student can pick it without knowing the idea. Some distractors should be plausible but wrong without absolute words.
The clue ('informs management, not that it replaces it') directly rules out one distractor and points to the overstated-claim pattern, which narrows the choice too far.

b.q: A fire agency in New South Wales asks a group of Aboriginal rangers to help plan fire management in a forest. Why is this a sensible step?

They burn with large, hot fires that clear the forest floor
Their fire methods come from recent trials in this forest
